content: Sleight of Mouth is a structured system of linguistic patterns designed to enhance persuasive communication. This concept was developed by Robert Dilts, who analyzed and modeled the argumentation and persuasion techniques of Richard Bandler, one of the co-founders of Neuro-Linguistic Programming (NLP). By deconstructing these methods, Dilts identified 14 foundational patterns. Subsequently, other contributors, such as Steve and Connirae Andreas, expanded upon these original patterns by introducing additional ones. The primary goal of formalizing the study of influence within the NLP framework is to enable individuals to comprehend the mechanisms of persuasion and replicate these skills through the deliberate application of one or more Sleight of Mouth patterns. The term Sleight of Mouth is derived from the phrase Sleight of Hand, which refers to a magician's ability to perform seemingly impossible feats. Similarly, Sleight of Mouth involves skillfully influencing beliefs and perceptions through language. Beliefs Sleight of Mouth primarily focuses on influencing others by challenging and altering their beliefs. A belief, in its simplest form, is something an individual holds to be true, such as I believe there is a God. However, within the context of Sleight of Mouth, beliefs are understood through more specific frameworks, such as: Complex Equivalence: This is the idea that X equals Y or that X is equivalent to Y. Cause-Effect: This suggests that X causes Y or that X results in Y. For example: You’re late again, which means you don’t love me. (This is not merely a belief that you don’t love me, but rather a conclusion drawn from the perceived cause-effect relationship of being late.) I am not going to do that—I am not that kind of person. (This reflects a belief tied to identity and self-perception.) Patterns The key patterns of Sleight of Mouth are outlined below. However, a deeper understanding is achieved by examining examples and observing how these patterns are applied in practice. 1. Intent: Focus on the intention behind the statement. This can involve highlighting the positive intent behind the belief or challenging the negative intent. 2. Consequences: Identify a consequence (even an unintended one) that challenges the belief. 3. Another Outcome: Suggest an alternative perspective or outcome that reframes the belief. 4. Counterexample: Present an exception where the belief or statement would not hold true, thereby questioning its validity. 5. Apply to Self: Redirect the statement back to the person making it, implying that the consequence they suggest for you actually applies to them. 6. Reality Strategy: Challenge the belief by questioning the evidence or perceptions that led to it. Ask how they know their belief is true or what aspects of the belief are genuinely at issue. 7. Model of the World: Suggest that their statement is a metaphor for something else, rather than a literal truth. 8. Meta Frame: Challenge the underlying assumptions of the belief rather than the belief itself. Point out that their belief presupposes something that may not be valid. 9. Change Frame Size: Expand or reduce the implications of the belief to a larger or smaller scale, or to a longer or shorter time frame. 10. Hierarchy of Criteria: Challenge the belief by appealing to higher or more important criteria, suggesting that there are more significant considerations. 11. Chunk Down: Focus on a specific element of the belief and challenge it. 12. Chunk Up: Generalize the belief to challenge its broader implications. 13. Metaphor/Analogy: Use a metaphor or analogy to illustrate why the belief may not hold true. 14. Redefine: Use similar language to restate the belief in a way that changes its implications. Example Applications Example 1: You’re late again, which means you don’t love me. Intent: I’m glad you care enough about me to be concerned about that. Consequences: You’re just trying to get me to always fit within your timetable. Another Outcome: Would you have preferred me to cancel our dinner if I knew I was going to be late? Counterexample: Have you ever loved someone but still been late? Apply to Self: An accusation like that makes it sound like you don’t love me. Reality Strategy: How did you come to that conclusion? Has someone accused you of something similar in the past? Model of the World: I’m guessing it’s not so much that I’m late, but you’re concerned about me not focusing on the little things in our relationship. Meta Frame: Where did you learn that being on time equates to love? Are you saying that none of them care? Hierarchy of Criteria: Isn’t it more important that I actually made the effort to get here, in spite of everything that happened along the way? Chunk Down: What about all the times I have been on time? Chunk Up: You’re judging an entire relationship based on time-keeping? Metaphor/Analogy: Isn’t that like saying if you don’t cook for me every time, you don’t love me? Redefine: You’re saying a small delay defines an entire relationship? Example 2: I am not going to do that—I am not that kind of person. Intent: It’s great that you make decisions based on how you see yourself as a person. Consequences: Why are you focused on decisions that avoid you having to leave the house? Another Outcome: But if you don’t do that, can you ever hope to develop into the person you’d like to become? Counterexample: Have you ever done something that you didn’t think was ‘you,’ yet you really enjoyed it? Apply to Self: You’re not the kind of person to pre-judge, yet here you are—pre-judging. Reality Strategy: And exactly what kind of person do you have to be to do that kind of thing? Model of the World: Does everyone who is afraid to try something new say that? Meta Frame: You’re only saying that because you’re afraid of what others might think. Change Frame Size: Yeah, that’s right. Only a truly open-minded person would do that. Hierarchy of Criteria: What’s more important, trying new things and expanding your horizons or being safe and restricted in your tiny comfort zone? Chunk Down: What kind of person would that make you, specifically? Chunk Up: Do you always get out of trying new things by making excuses? Metaphor/Analogy: People aren’t born as astronauts. Redefine: You don’t have to tie up your identity with a few actions.
